Transcript: (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect)
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to do a quick sprint pulse, how are we seeing the week, Samir?
[00:12] Samir Khan: yeah thanks Maya. uh quick context, we had a surprise spike last Friday and the burst took us to 3x usual, we saw latency creep up on tail percentiles and cost spiked. we want to figure out guardrails so that customer-facing flows keep sub-200ms while not blowing budget.
[00:30] Jorge Ramos: got it. just to confirm — that was hosted mode, not dedicated, right?
[00:35] Samir Khan: correct, hosted. we're still evaluating Dedicated but want to understand cost tradeoffs before committing.
[00:40] Aisha Rahman: and if I can add, we saw some token blowup during multi-turn chat — prefix reuse wasn't kicking in for a subset of sessions. unsure if it's client side or server side cache misses.
[00:52] Lena Ortiz: yeah we suspected our client sometimes creates slightly different prompt IDs which prevents prefix/K V cache hits. also some requests bypassed batching because of sticky low latency routing.
[01:05] Jorge Ramos: interesting. we can look at the batching stats and also how your routing policy is configured. Redwood has an autoscale A/B policy we can run that keeps a safety cap per route — basically throttle-to-keep-latency.
[01:20] Chris Park: from finance perspective, we need a clear model: if spikes happen 2-3x weekly what does that look like dollars-wise for burst vs a small reserved pool?
[01:30] Maya Patel: absolutely. we'll send a cost-scenario spreadsheet. quick preview: burst is cheaper at low frequency spikes but becomes more expensive if sustained. reserved capacity gives you predictable unit cost and lower tail latency. we can model your 95th/99th distributions into both.
[01:45] Samir Khan: can you show an example with autoscale that has fallback to a cheaper quantized model when tail is bad? we need graceful degradation for non-critical requests.
[01:54] Jorge Ramos: yes we have model variant routing — policy-based fallback to a quantized gptx-13q (note: auto transcript might get the model name slightly off) that keeps latency but reduces token cost. for critical flows you can pin to standard profile and have quota/alerting.
[02:10] Lena Ortiz: ok but how does that affect stateful multi-turn chats? if we fallback model, KV cache formats differ. do we lose context?
[02:18] Jorge Ramos: good question. for model variant fallback we keep the same kv cache format when models are from the same family; if you fallback to a different arch there is some context conversion loss. we typically do prefix-only caching to keep continuity, and have a short cold-start penalty.
[02:35] Samir Khan: that last bit — cold start — that's what bit us. we saw a 2s tail occasionally.
[02:40] Jorge Ramos: right, cold starts happen when scale jumps and a new worker spins up, we have autoscale warmers and pre-warm policies. one thing to tune is the warm-up concurrency and the kv cache prefetch window.
[02:53] Maya Patel: also there's a queueing knob to smooth abrupt bursts so you don't spin up too many small workers and pay more; it's a latency vs cost tradeoff.
[03:02] Chris Park: can Redwood provide a sample pricing calc showing that exact scenario? e.g., 3x spike for 30 minutes, three times a week.
[03:12] Maya Patel: yes, that's in the next steps. we'll produce two scenarios: burst-only and small reserved + burst overlay and show delta.
[03:20] Samir Khan: great. on security, compliance team wants SOC2 Type II evidence and example audit logs for admin actions and model calls. plus KMS integration for PII encryption.
[03:31] Aisha Rahman: we have a security pack — but I'll double-check the audit log retention examples. we can share SSO docs for SAML and how RBAC maps to console roles.
[03:40] Lena Ortiz: also data residency — some EU traffic needs to avoid US regions; how's routing for geo constrained requests?
[03:47] Jorge Ramos: we support region pinning and smart routing. requests can be routed by policy and we can fallback to nearest compatible region in an outage. we log region fallbacks for compliance.
[03:58] Samir Khan: perfect. back to ops — is there a simple guardrail recommended? like set autoscale upper bound at 2x baseline and queue length threshold T, and then fallback model at 90th latency of 300ms?
[04:10] Jorge Ramos: that's a reasonable starting point. suggested: upper bound 2.5x, warmup concurrency 3, queue threshold 25ms, and fallback model on p99 > 400ms. fine tune after pilot.
[04:22] Maya Patel: we'll propose a default playbook and you'll tell us which routes are critical vs opportunistic.
[04:28] Chris Park: one more on billing — any hidden costs like KV cache egress or long-lived sessions? we need to avoid surprises.
[04:36] Maya Patel: KV cache itself is included, but long-lived sessions that pin resources could increase reserved capacity needs. we'll call that out in the cost sheet.
[04:45] Samir Khan: ok. timeline: we want a pilot stress run next week to see heatmaps. can Redwood run a synthetic load against our staging endpoints?
[04:53] Jorge Ramos: yes, we can coordinate; we'll need traffic patterns and sample tokens.
[04:58] Samir Khan: I'll get that by Monday.
[05:00] Maya Patel: great. quick note — Chris, finance — we can also show amortized cost if you buy a 3-month reserved block vs pay-as-you-go.
[05:07] Chris Park: that would be helpful.
[05:10] (small side chatter about calendar invites and timezone snafu)
[05:35] Lena Ortiz: there was also a thing where our logs showed 7% requests returning 429 during the spike. is that rate limit or endpoint protection?
[05:43] Jorge Ramos: 429s usually from rate limiting at route level; can be tuned per API key or per-user. we can also enable soft-throttling to shift user experience rather than hard 429s.
[05:55] Samir Khan: soft throttle sounds better. our mobile app needs graceful slowdown not errors.
[06:02] Aisha Rahman: we can configure blue/green policies for route-level throttles and test in staging.
[06:10] Maya Patel: circling back to security review — we'll attach SOC2 scan excerpts, KMS integration doc, and sample audit logs to the follow-up email.
[06:19] Chris Park: timeline for that?
[06:22] Aisha Rahman: aiming to send by EOD Tuesday.
[06:25] Samir Khan: good.
[06:28] (brief pause)
[06:35] Jorge Ramos: on the technical side I'll run the autoscale playbook against your staging metrics and share the aggregated warmup and queue charts, should take about 48 hours once I have the samples.
[06:48] Samir Khan: and we'll provide the traffic profiles and sample chat prompts — note: some prompts include user PII so we'll put placeholders.
[06:57] Maya Patel: perfect. next, we discussed fallbacks to quantized models — do you want that enabled for all non-critical routes?
[07:05] Lena Ortiz: yes for experimentation, but critical transactional flows should never fallback.
[07:10] Jorge Ramos: we'll mark routes accordingly.
[07:13] Maya Patel: quick recap then: Redwood sends pricing scenarios + security pack; SE runs autoscale playbook and shares logs; BlueFjord provides traffic patterns and sample tokens; schedule pilot stress run week of 8/17. any objections?
[07:30] Samir Khan: none.
[07:33] Chris Park: agree.
[07:35] Lena Ortiz: good.
[07:37] Maya Patel: last thing — competitors. you mentioned considering Bedrock and Anthropic — any strong leaning?
[07:43] Samir Khan: Bedrock for some legacy integrations but Anthropic for safety features; we want to keep options open but favor predictable economics.
[07:53] Maya Patel: understood. we'll include a short comparison table in the follow up.
[07:58] (wrap-up comments)
[08:05] Maya Patel: thanks everyone. I'll send notes and the attachments within 48 hours.
[08:10] Jorge Ramos: thanks, talk soon.
